subject: history_social
passage: In 1833 a ship called the Tuscany left Boston carrying about 180 tons of ice cut from New England ponds, bound for Calcutta, a voyage of four months that crossed the equator twice. Many observers expected the cargo to arrive as water. Instead, more than half of it reached India still frozen, and the city soon built a special ice house to store later shipments. The trade depended on an unglamorous material: sawdust. Packed around the blocks, it slowed melting enough to make such voyages possible, and because New England's lumber mills produced it as waste, it cost shippers almost nothing. For decades, until machines that manufactured ice became common later in the century, much of Calcutta's ice came from frozen ponds on the other side of the world.
stem: According to the text, why was sawdust important to the ice trade between Boston and Calcutta?

choices.A: It replaced the ice house that Calcutta had built to store the shipments that came later.
choices.B: It let ships carry ice across the equator twice without needing to stop at any port along the way.
choices.C: It slowed the melting of the ice on long voyages while costing shippers very little to obtain.
choices.D: It was later replaced on ships by machines that kept the ice frozen for the whole voyage.

explanation.why: The text says that sawdust, "packed around the blocks, ... slowed melting enough to make such voyages possible," and that because lumber mills "produced it as waste, it cost shippers almost nothing." Both effectiveness and low cost made it important.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The ice house stored ice in Calcutta; sawdust did not replace it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never discusses stopping at ports during the voyage.
explanation.C: Correct. This combines the two reasons the text gives: sawdust slowed melting, and it was nearly free.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The machines mentioned manufactured ice, ending the trade; the text never says they were used on ships.
